qs.q: An infant post-repair of oesophageal atresia develops severe, medically refractory gastro-oesophageal reflux disease causing recurrent aspiration and oesophagitis. Which surgical procedure is indicated if acid suppression fails?
qs.e: Fundoplication is used to treat gastro-oesophageal reflux when medical acid suppression is inadequate, especially after oesophageal replacement. Heller myotomy is used for achalasia, not reflux.

qs.q: A patient presents with symptoms of GERD. In mild cases of reflux oesophagitis, what is the predominant endoscopic and histological appearance of the distal esophageal mucosa?
o: Marked basal zone hypoplasia and absent lamina propria papillae
Extensive mucosal necrosis with fungal hyphae invasion
Simple hyperaemia with often unremarkable mucosal histology
qs.e: In mild GERD, the only alteration may be simple hyperaemia (redness on endoscopy), and mucosal histology is often unremarkable. Histological hallmarks like basal zone hyperplasia appear in more significant, severe disease.

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with odynophagia and white plaques on endoscopy – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Obtain oesophageal biopsy to confirm Candida versus viral infection; guides antifungal versus antiviral therapy.

How does the Los Angeles classification influence management decisions? — Higher grades (C‑D) often require high‑dose PPI, possible sucralfate, and closer follow‑up; lower grades may respond to lifestyle measures alone.

You suspect TB oesitis in a patient with chronic cough and dysphagia; endoscopy is unavailable. What bedside investigation helps and what would you do with a positive result? — Perform a chest X‑ray; if mediastinal widening or pulmonary infiltrates suggest TB, start anti‑TB therapy while arranging referral for endoscopy.

A child presents with progressive dysphagia and a history of frequent use of herbal bitter kola. Which condition should you consider and what is the key management step? — Caustic oesophagitis; immediate cessation of the herb, initiate PPI, and arrange endoscopic assessment for stricture risk.
Why is it unsafe to give NSAIDs to a patient with severe reflux oesophagitis? — NSAIDs impair mucosal prostaglandin synthesis, worsening ulceration and increasing bleeding risk.

What complication distinguishes oesophageal perforation from severe ulceration on examination? — Subcutaneous emphysema and crepitus in the neck/chest indicate perforation, requiring urgent surgical review.

A patient with known portal hypertension presents with haematemesis. How do you differentiate variceal bleed from oesophagitis bleed? — Endoscopy shows bluish, tortuous veins (varices) versus erosive mucosal breaks; variceal bleed mandates vasoactive drugs and band ligation.
ai.title: Oesophagitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Inflammation of the oesophageal mucosa caused by reflux, infection, medication or systemic disease. Diagnosis relies on history, endoscopy and selective tests, with severity staged to guide therapy.

b: Endoscopy is the gold‑standard; look for erythema, erosions, ulcerations, white plaques.
Biopsy is reserved for suspected infection, eosinophilic oesophagitis or malignancy.
sections.p: Oesophagitis is mucosal inflammation of the oesophagus confirmed by endoscopic visualisation of erosions, ulceration or ulcerated plaques, or by histology when needed.

b: LA A: one or more mucosal breaks ≤5 mm, not extending between the tops of two mucosal folds.
LA B: one or more breaks >5 mm, but not continuous between folds.
LA C: at least one continuous break spanning ≥2 folds.
LA D: extensive mucosal loss involving >75 % of the circumference.
sections.p: The Los Angeles (LA) classification, originally for reflux oesophagitis, is widely used and applicable to other aetiologies.

b: Gastro‑oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) – most common overall.
Infectious: Candida (especially HIV), Herpes simplex, Cytomegalovirus – consider in immunosuppressed.
Medication‑induced: doxycycline, tetracyclines, bisphosphonates, NSAIDs, iron tablets – often from improper administration.
Tuberculosis oesitis – rare but reported with pulmonary TB.
Schistosomiasis (S. mansoni) – can cause chronic ulcerative lesions.
Herbal remedies (e.g., bitter kola) – direct caustic injury.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the hierarchy of aetiologies differs from high‑income countries.

b: Odynophagia – pain on swallowing, worsens with liquids then solids.
Dysphagia – progressive difficulty, first solids then liquids in severe disease.
Retrosternal burning – may mimic heartburn.
Weight loss, fever, night sweats – red flags for infection or malignancy.
sections.p: Patients usually present with odynophagia, dysphagia and retrosternal pain; systemic signs appear with infection or severe ulceration.
Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, use clinical judgment and alternative bedside tools.

t.b: What is the mucosal appearance and severity? – Direct visual staging; guides therapy and need for biopsy.
Is there an infectious or eosinophilic cause? – Histology shows Candida hyphae, viral inclusions, eosinophils; confirms diagnosis.
Is immunosuppression present? – Positive result raises suspicion for opportunistic infection; start appropriate prophylaxis.
Is there mediastinal widening or pulmonary TB? – Suggests TB oesitis or complications; may prompt empirical anti‑TB therapy.
Is there a stricture or perforation? – Shows narrowing, ulcer crater; helps plan safe endoscopy.

b: Severe odynophagia with inability to swallow fluids – risk of dehydration.
Upper GI bleed (hematemesis, melena) – consider ulceration or varices.
Perforation – sudden severe chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema.
Stricture formation – progressive dysphagia after healing.
sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent intervention.

b: Proton‑pump inhibitor (PPI) – reduces acid exposure; first‑line for reflux‑related disease.
Topical sucralfate slurry – coats ulcerated mucosa; useful when PPIs unavailable.
Antifungal (e.g., fluconazole) for Candida – only after confirming infection.
Acyclovir/IV ganciclovir for HSV/CMV – reserved for immunocompromised with proven virus.
Discontinue offending medication; advise upright posture with water for tablets.
Nutritional support – oral liquids, then soft diet; consider nasogastric feeding if severe.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the mucosa and control symptoms; avoid drugs that worsen injury.

b: Weight‑bearing head‑up position after taking pills; plenty of water.
Avoid late‑night meals, alcohol, smoking – reduce reflux.
Screen for HIV and TB in high‑risk patients; treat accordingly.
Educate on safe use of herbal preparations.
sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 4–6 weeks with repeat endoscopy if symptoms persist; counsel on lifestyle and medication safety.

b: Peptic ulcer disease of the distal oesophagus – usually acid‑related but may present with similar pain.
Mallory‑Weiss tear – mucosal laceration after retching, causes haematemesis.
Esophageal varices – dilated veins that bleed; look for bluish bulging veins rather than erosions.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic oesophagitis clinically or endoscopically.

b: Normal endoscopy does not exclude eosinophilic oesophagitis – need biopsies.
Negative Candida culture from saliva may be false; tissue biopsy is definitive.
PPI use can mask ulceration, leading to under‑staging.
sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation that may mask or exaggerate disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Vomiting of blood or coffee‑ground material
Sudden severe chest pain with crepitus
Persistent fever or weight loss >5 % in 1 month
